title: Closed-loop control for two-qubit gates with trapped ions
authors: Eduardo J. Páez, Seyed Shakib Vedaie, Barry C. Sanders
abstract: State-of-the-art two-qubit gates with trapped ions employ open-loop control that rely on simplified models to precompute control sequences. Our aim is to introduce closed-loop control for two-qubit gates to correct disturbances as they occur during the gate implementation. We introduce a spectator ion into the ion chain used for quantum logic processing, where it couples with the other ions through collective motional modes. The spectator ion's position is continuously monitored by driving dipole transitions and detecting the resultant fluorescence. We show that incorporating a spectator ion is feasible for linear Paul trap implementations and is expected to reduce the two-qubit gate Bell-state preparation infidelity by an order of magnitude with the deleterious effects of position monitoring being negligible compared to the thermal effects that exist in the system, even in the absence of the spectator ions. Mathematically, we describe driven ion-trap dynamics, including the spectator ion, by a stochastic quantum master equation involving the amplitude-modulation multimode-motional coupling gate, motional drift, thermal effects, recoil from photon scattering, spontaneous decay, and light shift. Our on-the-fly control method employs reinforcement learning with the reward function based on the actual geometric phase of the spectator ion. A key advantage of our approach is that we introduce a control method that involves `learning' and correcting disturbances happening in the trap on-the-fly, thus achieving high-fidelity gates. Our approach will lead to a significantly higher two-qubit gate fidelity at a reduced calibration overhead owing to the small parameter drift in the control system.
summary: The paper introduces a novel closed-loop control scheme for two-qubit gates in trapped ion systems, moving beyond simplified open-loop models that fail under noise. By continuously monitoring an ancillary 'spectator ion' and employing reinforcement learning, the system can correct disturbances in real time. This method promises significantly higher gate fidelity with reduced calibration overhead.
main_problem: The primary goal is to improve the fidelity of two-qubit gates (2QG) in trapped ions by replacing unreliable open-loop control with a real-time, closed-loop feedback mechanism.
main_result: A proposed Closed-Loop Position Monitoring (CLPM) scheme, utilizing reinforcement learning on a spectator ion's position, is shown to significantly reduce 2QG gate infidelity compared to state-of-the-art methods.
method: The approach combines quantum trajectory theory (QTT) with reinforcement learning (RL), where an RL agent learns the optimal control sequence by maximizing a reward function based on the spectator ion's geometric phase.
model_or_system: The system is trapped ions in a linear Paul trap, modeled using a stochastic quantum master equation that accounts for motional drift, thermal effects, and photon scattering. A key addition is monitoring an ancillary 'spectator ion' via fluorescence detection.
key_observables: Two-qubit gate fidelity ($I$), the geometric phase of the spectator ion ($\chi_{qr}$), and the position/fluorescence signal from the spectator ion.
important_parameters: Gate duration ($	au_g$), required precision (e.g., $0.3\Delta x_0$ resolution), and noise sources like motional heating or trap voltage fluctuations ($\delta f$).
main_assumptions: The feasibility of continuous position monitoring is assumed, and the control system's ability to process real-time feedback from the measured fluorescence signal is central.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate phase-space trajectories for ion chains under various gate schemes (SotA vs. proposed), showing how closed loops imply minimal residual correlation between electronic states and motional modes.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the limitations of open-loop control, then mathematically modeling the full dynamics using a stochastic master equation incorporating monitoring terms. It details the RL framework for on-the-fly correction, culminating in performance comparisons showing the superiority of the closed-loop approach.
why_interesting: This work represents a significant step toward fault-tolerant quantum computation by addressing environmental noise dynamically. The integration of machine learning (RL) directly into the control loop for physical hardware like trapped ions is highly relevant to modern AMO research.

Figure 2. Diagram of the CLPM-scheme. A three-ion chain is illustrated, where the orange dots represent gate ions and the green dot represents the spectator ion. The spectator ion is illuminated with an external coherent laser coupled to the 2S1/2 – 2P1/2 transition, illustrated as a diagonal blue cone-like shape. An array of lenses and a back mirror collect and su- perpose the fluorescence light to undergo a two-channel time- correlated single-photon counting (TCSPC) setup. The out- put signal is sent to a FPGA for post-processing. The global and bichromatic Raman beams are not shown for simplicity.
